h1: 10 Best Things to Do in Yasothon
intro: Yasothon is a small Isan town packed with character, from the heart of the city all the way out to the open fields — a 19-metre giant-toad building, a colourful Sino-European old shophouse district, Thailand's largest wooden Christian church, an ancient stupa in the middle of rice paddies tied to a beloved local legend, and a hundred-rai red lotus field in the cool season. We've rounded up the 10 attractions people talk about most, complete with entry fees, locations, and trip-planning tips. Whether you're touring the city in a single day or driving out to catch the wooden church and the red lotus field overnight, it's all doable.
chips: 🏯 Phra That Kong Khao Noi in the fields
⛪ Song Yae Wooden Church, Thailand's largest

blocks.html:
Yasothon's charm is "an easygoing small town where every highlight still carries a whiff of legend and faith." Many of the standout spots cluster around the centre of town near Phaya Thaen Park, the city's green lung where the evening breeze is cool enough for a walk or a jog. Right next to it sits the Phaya Khankhak Toad Museum, a giant toad-shaped building as tall as a five-storey block that tells the legend of Phaya Khankhak and the Bun Bang Fai rocket festival — the very thing that made Yasothon famous nationwide. A short walk further into the municipal area brings you to the Ban Sing Tha old town, rows of pastel-painted Sino-European shophouses you can photograph for free, block after block. For those into spirituality and culture, Wat Mahathat, the city's guardian temple, holds Phra That Anon and the Dewdrop Buddha for you to pay respects to. There's something here for landmark chasers, old-town wanderers, nature lovers, and the faithful alike.

This list also includes stops you shouldn't skip on a Yasothon trip — like Phra That Kong Khao Noi, standing amid rice fields and tied to the "child who killed his mother" legend known across the whole Isan region; Ban Song Yae Christian Church in Thai Charoen district, Thailand's largest wooden church, nearly a century old and built entirely of hardwood; the 100-plus-rai red lotus field, the province's signature flower, blooming beautifully on cool-season mornings from December into early the following year; Wat Phra Phutthabat Yasothon in Maha Chana Chai with its white-and-blue ordination hall and a large white jade Buddha image; and rounding things off, Phu Phra Cave in Loeng Nok Tha and Dong Mueang Toei, an ancient Khmer-Dvaravati-era community also linked to the Kong Khao Noi legend. Scroll down for the details on each spot and build your own route.

blocks.name: Phaya Khankhak Toad Museum (Vimarn Phaya Thaen)
blocks.area: Nai Mueang Subdistrict, Mueang Yasothon District
blocks.signature: A 19-metre giant-toad-shaped building as tall as a 5-storey block, telling the legend of Phaya Khankhak and the Bun Bang Fai festival, next to the eye-catching golden Vimarn Phaya Thaen
blocks.descHtml:
If you come to Yasothon and skip the giant toad-shaped building by the Lam Thuan reservoir, you haven't really visited. The Phaya Khankhak Toad Museum is a 19-metre-tall "toad" (Phaya Khankhak in the Isan dialect) building, as tall as a five-storey block, crouched proudly in the middle of Phaya Thaen Park — a landmark so striking that drivers passing by slow down to look. Next to it is the gleaming golden Vimarn Phaya Thaen, which makes the whole corner even more eye-catching. It's a great fit for families bringing kids to learn, photographers, and anyone who wants to understand the legend of Phaya Khankhak and Phaya Thaen, the origin story behind the province's famous Bun Bang Fai rocket festival.

The highlight is working your way up floor by floor. The ground floor tells the history of Yasothon city, and the floors above cover the legends of Phaya Thaen and Phaya Khankhak, the Bun Bang Fai tradition, and the town's identity, with models, exhibits, and fun facts about hundreds of toad species that get kids excited. What you really shouldn't miss is climbing all the way up to the toad's "mouth" at the very top — a 360-degree viewpoint over the city of Yasothon. Many reviewers say that view up top is genuinely the star of the show. Outside, there's a model Bun Bang Fai procession and plenty more photo spots.

It's very easy on the wallet — 40 baht for adults, 20 baht for children — and takes about 1-2 hours to see everything. It's open Wednesday-Friday roughly 10:00 am-4:30 pm, and Saturday-Sunday plus public holidays 9:30 am-5:30 pm, closed on Tuesdays (unless it falls on a public holiday). It sits within the Yasothon municipal area in Nai Mueang Subdistrict, easy to reach, with parking on site.

One thing worth knowing: opening hours are listed slightly differently across sources, so it's worth calling ahead if you're planning to visit on a weekday, and avoid Tuesdays since it's closed. The building itself and the viewpoint are the real draw, though some reviews note the surrounding grounds could be kept up better. Even so, as the province's signature symbol with a look you won't find anywhere else, this is one of Yasothon's top check-in spots and shouldn't be missed.
mustOrder: Photograph the 19-metre giant-toad building
Climb to the top-floor Yasothon city viewpoint (the toad's mouth)
See the Phaya Khankhak-Phaya Thaen legend exhibit + Bun Bang Fai displays
Stop by the golden Vimarn Phaya Thaen next door
blocks.hours: Wed-Fri 10:00 am-4:30 pm · Sat-Sun/holidays 9:30 am-5:30 pm · closed Tuesdays
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Nori808 / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

blocks.name: Phra That Kong Khao Noi
blocks.area: Tat Thong Subdistrict, Mueang Yasothon District, Yasothon
blocks.signature: An old rice-basket-shaped stupa standing in open rice fields, tied to the folk legend of 'the child who killed his mother,' known across all of Isan
blocks.descHtml:
Mention Yasothon, and besides the rocket festival, almost every Isan person will think of "Phra That Kong Khao Noi," because it's tied to the folk legend of "Kong Khao Noi Kha Mae" (the little rice basket that led to a mother's death), passed down through generations. The story goes that a farmer's son, starving while working the fields, saw his mother arrive late with what looked like a tiny basket of rice, flew into a blind rage, and killed her — only to find, once he actually ate, that there was rice left over. Overcome with remorse, he built a stupa shaped like a rice basket to atone for his sin. The actual stupa is an old brick structure, square with a pointed spire, standing prominently amid the rice paddies — a great fit for anyone who loves a place with a story, history buffs, and people who just want to stop, pay respects, and capture a beautiful shot.

The must-see highlight is the old stupa standing in the open fields — the photos are stunning in the late afternoon, when golden light falls across the paddies. Many reviews describe the atmosphere as romantic and peaceful. Another popular custom here is making a vow and, once it's fulfilled, leaving a "buffalo statue" as an offering — you'll see rows of these placed around the site, a signature image of this spot. For anyone into little-known trivia, there are actually two stupas of this kind in the Tat Thong area — one at Wat Thung Sadao and one at Ban Tat Thong — just a few kilometres apart, so you can visit both.

Money-wise, it couldn't be easier: entry is free, with no admission charge, open around the clock. There's a parking area, restrooms, and local vendors selling regional snacks and souvenirs nearby, so the whole visit costs little more than a drink and a snack. It's located amid the rice fields of Tat Thong Subdistrict, Mueang Yasothon District, about 9 km from the city centre — follow Chaeng Sanit Road (Highway 23) toward Kham Khuean Kaeo, then turn into the village. It's an easy drive with straightforward parking.

Honestly, one thing to know: online review scores sit around 3.6-3.7, with some reviewers noting the upkeep could be better. If you're expecting something grand, it may feel plainer than you imagined. But if you're here for a genuine taste of Isan folklore, a photo of the old stupa in the fields, and a moment to pay your respects, this place has an atmosphere you won't find anywhere else. We'd recommend visiting in the late afternoon to avoid the midday heat, when the light is at its best.
mustOrder: The old brick, rice-basket-shaped stupa in the open fields
Photos in the late-afternoon golden light
The 'Kong Khao Noi Kha Mae' legend + votive buffalo statues
The twin stupa at nearby Wat Thung Sadao
blocks.bestFor: Legend and history lovers, and photos of the stupa in the fields during evening light
blocks.libCredit: Photo by Supanut Arunoprayote / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

blocks.name: Ban Sing Tha Old Town
blocks.signature: Rows of brightly coloured Sino-European shophouses you can photograph throughout the district, free to visit
blocks.descHtml:
If you like strolling through old districts and photographing historic buildings at an unhurried pace, the Ban Sing Tha old town in the heart of Yasothon municipality is a must-visit. This area was once a trading district along the Chi River dating back to the city's founding. When French and Chinese-Vietnamese merchants arrived, the shophouses took on a Sino-European style (many compare it to the Sino-Portuguese architecture of Phuket), painted in bright pastel colours with folding wooden shutters and stucco detailing that's held up remarkably well. You can photograph the whole district for free.

The highlight is walking along and admiring the old buildings on both sides of Si Sunthon Road, Nakhon Thoom Road, Uthai Ramrit Road, and Witthaya Thamrong Road, each stretch with its own distinct character — from a pink-and-orange Sino-style coffee shop building to a white carved wooden shophouse that once sold rice, right down to the Singha Roundabout, the district's signature check-in spot. For the full atmosphere, stop by the Ban Sing Tha Old Town Museum, a white two-storey colonial building with air conditioning that presents Yasothon's history through interactive displays — also free to enter. Many reviewers say wearing white or cream tones makes for photos that blend beautifully with the buildings.

The overall vibe is slow-living — locals go about their lives simply, without the crowds — so it's best visited in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is soft and it's not too hot. Along the way, you can also try local specialties like fermented fish (pla som) and Yasothon-style lod chong dessert. Set aside one to two hours; the district sits within the municipal area, so it's easy to reach with convenient parking, open for walking any day (the museum itself is open roughly 8:30 am-4:30 pm), and free to enter.

People love it because it's a genuinely lived-in old town, not staged for tourists — you can wander at ease and come away with great photos without much planning. One thing to note: some of the shops in the district are still occupied homes, so be a little mindful when taking photos, and some shops may be closed on weekdays — visit on a weekend if you want more buzz.
mustOrder: Walk and photograph the pastel Sino-European shophouses along Si Sunthon Road
Check in at the Singha Roundabout, the district's landmark
Visit the Ban Sing Tha Old Town Museum (free)
Try the famous local fermented fish and lod chong dessert
blocks.bestFor: Cafe-hoppers and retro-photo lovers wanting a relaxed morning/late-afternoon stroll
blocks.hours: Open daily for walking · museum ~8:30 am-4:30 pm

blocks.name: Ho Trai, Wat Sa Trai Nurak (Wat Ban Na Wiang)
blocks.signature: An old wooden scripture library standing in the middle of a pond, built with Isan-Lan Xang craftsmanship blended with Tai Yai influence
blocks.priceRange: Grounds free (museum has an entry fee)
blocks.descHtml:
If you like quiet places with a story stretching back a hundred years, the Ho Trai (scripture library) at Wat Sa Trai Nurak in Ban Na Wiang, Sai Mun District, is a spot worth the detour. The library itself is a small wooden pavilion standing in the middle of a pond, reached only by a narrow wooden footbridge — seen from the water's edge, it looks like an old painting, the wooden roof's reflection resting on the still surface. What makes it special is that it wasn't built over water purely for beauty: people in the past used the water as a barrier against ants and termites, since the building once held large collections of palm-leaf Tripitaka manuscripts — exactly the kind of thing insects love to eat. Placing the library in the middle of a pond was simple folk wisdom that genuinely worked.

The craftsmanship here is well worth a close look. The whole structure is timber, resting on dozens of round wooden columns, with a tiered gabled roof rising in layers and overhanging eaves projecting on all four sides, covered in small wooden roof shingles — an Isan-Lan Xang style influenced by Tai Yai and Burmese art, giving the roofline a shape quite different from typical Isan temples. If you enjoy noticing old woodworking details, walk around and you'll spot the joinery and the deliberate, unhurried layering of the roof tiers.

Its age is no small thing either — this scripture library is said to date back to roughly the 18th-19th century Buddhist Era, tied to stories of people migrating from the Vientiane side to settle here. It's been restored several times over the past hundred-plus years, and in 1990 the Fine Arts Department registered it as a national ancient monument. Today it's cared for as a community historical scripture-library museum, so when you visit, please help preserve it — don't climb on or handle the wooden structure roughly, so this piece of history can last much longer.

A visit here suits anyone who wants a change of pace from grand temples and to see something genuinely rare up close. It doesn't take long — walk around the pond taking photos, listen to stories from locals if a caretaker is around, then move comfortably on to your next Yasothon stop. It's about 25 km from Yasothon city, and we'd recommend driving yourself, since public transport doesn't reach it easily. Morning or evening, when the light is soft, makes for the best photos, and modest dress is appropriate since it's temple grounds. For exact entry fees or opening hours, it's best to check with locals again before you go.
mustOrder: The wooden scripture library standing in the middle of the pond
The tiered gabled roof in Tai Yai style
Century-old woodworking craftsmanship
The former storage for ancient palm-leaf manuscripts
blocks.bestFor: History lovers and fans of quiet, old-timber craftsmanship

blocks.name: Wat Mahathat Yasothon
blocks.signature: The city's guardian temple, home to Phra That Anon and the Dewdrop Buddha, the spiritual centre of Yasothon locals
blocks.descHtml:
If you want to truly understand Yasothon, start at Wat Mahathat, a royal temple at the heart of the old town and the city's guardian temple since Yasothon's founding. It's not a grand, imposing temple, but one the people of Yasothon hold dear with their whole heart — a great fit for temple-goers, history lovers, and travellers wanting to check off the city's key landmark in one stop. A walk around doesn't take long, but you'll come away with both merit and stories.

The must-see highlight is "Phra That Anon," or Phra That Yasothon, a square, spired stupa resembling Phra That Phanom, standing prominently in front of the ordination hall. It's an ancient Isan stupa believed to enshrine relics of the Buddha's disciple Ananda — reportedly the only one of its kind in Thailand. Another piece many visitors make a point of paying respects to is the "Dewdrop Buddha" (Phra Phutthabusayarat), a tiny, clear Chiang Saen-style Buddha image said to be the smallest crystal Buddha image in Thailand. Don't forget to also check out the wooden scripture library on the water, built to store palm-leaf manuscripts brought from Vientiane. The atmosphere is shaded and peaceful, and it's a pleasant place to wander and take photos.

Cost-wise, there's nothing to worry about — entry is free, with donations at your discretion. It's located right in the city centre, close to the market and morning food stalls, with convenient parking, and it's open for visits daily roughly 8:00 am-5:00 pm. We'd recommend going in the morning before the sun gets strong, for a comfortable walk and nice light. If you visit in early March, you'll catch the Phra That Anon Worship Festival, a major annual tradition that draws the whole province together — a lively event well worth timing your trip around.

This temple is popular because it brings together everything important about the city — a sacred stupa, a rare crystal Buddha, and old architecture, all in one place. Visitors consistently describe it as peaceful, with a genuinely sacred atmosphere, and truly the spiritual centre of the people of Yasothon. One small thing to know: as a sacred site, dress modestly, and note that the ordination hall or the area housing the crystal Buddha may not always be open. If you're set on paying respects to the actual image, it's worth asking temple staff first.
mustOrder: Phra That Anon, the ancient stupa said to enshrine Ananda's relics
The Dewdrop Buddha (Phra Phutthabusayarat), said to be Thailand's smallest crystal Buddha image
The wooden scripture library on the water
The Phra That Anon Worship Festival in early March

blocks.title: 🛏️ Where to Stay in Yasothon — Right in the City Near Phaya Thaen Park and the Old Town
blocks.text: To make the most of Yasothon, consider staying a night — you can stroll along Phaya Thaen Park in the evening, visit the Phaya Khankhak Museum while it's quiet, then head out the next morning to catch the red lotus field in full bloom. The most popular places to stay cluster in the city centre near Phaya Thaen Park and the Ban Sing Tha old town, within easy walking distance of cafes and food in the middle of town. There's a mix of city-centre hotels and simple, affordable places to stay. Pick a location close to whatever you want to see first thing in the morning for the best value — compare prices and reviews before you book.

blocks.name: Ban Song Yae Christian Church
blocks.area: Ban Song Yae, Kham Toei Subdistrict, Thai Charoen District, Yasothon
blocks.signature: Thailand's largest wooden Christian church, nearly 100 years old, with an all-hardwood structure
blocks.descHtml:
If you're after something truly unusual to see with your own eyes in Yasothon, "Ban Song Yae Christian Church," officially St. Michael the Archangel Church, is right near the top of the list. Its selling point is clear: it's the largest wooden Christian church in Thailand, nearly 100 years old. The building measures 16 metres wide and 57 metres long, standing on 360 hardwood columns of various sizes, and roofed with over 80,000 small wooden shingles — with almost no concrete used anywhere in the structure. What's fascinating is how well the design blends Thai architectural style with a Western church form. Step inside and it's quiet, shaded, and cool, with breezes filtering through the wooden slats. Anyone into architecture, history, or photography will find plenty to love.

The must-see moment is standing in the centre of the hall and looking up at the full timber column and beam structure — a sight that's genuinely hard to find elsewhere. From there, look around at the stained-glass windows lining the walls; when sunlight streams through, the colours cast beautifully across the wooden floor. Many reviews agree the atmosphere inside feels more solemn and peaceful than expected, and even non-Christians can walk through comfortably. Another popular photo angle is from outside, capturing the full length of the roofline, and there's a local legend about villagers fleeing ghost stories to settle here, giving the site a charm rooted in real history.

Cost is nothing to worry about — entry is free, with no admission charge, though there's a donation box for those who'd like to contribute to the church's upkeep. It's open for visits daily roughly 8:00 am-6:00 pm. Dress modestly and respectfully, since it's still an active church used for Mass. If you visit during a service, you can still admire the exterior. It's located in Ban Song Yae, Kham Toei Subdistrict, Thai Charoen District, a fair distance from Yasothon city — driving yourself is the most convenient option.

One thing to know: it's fairly remote with no direct public transport, so plan your route and fuel up beforehand. Late morning to early afternoon is when sunlight lights up the stained glass most beautifully. It's worth combining with other stops along the same route. If you enjoy quiet places with a story that aren't crowded, this one delivers, and it photographs beautifully from every angle.
mustOrder: Look up at the full timber column and beam structure in the hall
The stained glass when sunlight falls across the wooden floor
The full wooden roofline from outside
The legend behind the village's founding
blocks.bestFor: Architecture and history fans and photographers — go from late morning to afternoon to catch the light hitting the stained glass

blocks.name: Wat Phra Phutthabat Yasothon
blocks.signature: A white-and-blue ordination hall enshrining a footprint of the Buddha, a reclining Buddha, and a large white jade Buddha image
blocks.descHtml:
If you're heading toward Maha Chana Chai District, "Wat Phra Phutthabat Yasothon" is worth a stop. It's an old temple set on a sandy rise along the banks of the Chi River in Ban Nong Yang, Hua Mueang Subdistrict, about 6 km from Maha Chana Chai town centre. What people talk about most is the clean, white-and-blue ordination hall, which stands out beautifully against a clear sky. It's a great fit for temple-goers, those seeking merit, and anyone who prefers a quiet temple away from the crowds of the famous ones.

The must-see highlight is "Phra Phutthalokanat," the temple's principal Buddha image, carved entirely from white jade with a lap width of about 2.31 metres — reportedly the largest white-jade Buddha image in Thailand. The pale, milky jade has a genuinely calming quality. Another point of interest is a replica Buddha footprint enshrined on the sandy rise, and a meditating Buddha under a naga hood said to have been brought from Ayutthaya. Architecture fans will also enjoy the three-tiered Maha Chana Chai stupa, which houses a display of old Isan household items and stores the Tripitaka scriptures, open for visitors to explore.

Cost-wise, there's nothing to worry about — entry is free, with donations at your discretion, open daily during the daytime. The overall setting is shaded and pleasant, sitting right by the Chi River with a cooling breeze. Past visitors often describe it as peaceful, better suited to quiet reflection than to snapping photos. It's a temple much loved by both Yasothon locals and dharma-minded travellers seeking blessings.

A few things to know: the temple is fairly out of town, with the final stretch of road leading through a village, so a private car or motorbike is the most convenient way in. Dress modestly, as it's temple grounds, and if you want the best shots of the blue-and-white ordination hall, visit in the morning or late afternoon when the sun isn't too harsh. Altogether, it's a worthwhile stop if you're exploring the Maha Chana Chai side of Yasothon.
mustOrder: Phra Phutthalokanat, Thailand's largest white jade Buddha, inside the white-and-blue ordination hall
Pay respects at the replica Buddha footprint on the sandy rise by the Chi River
The three-tiered Maha Chana Chai stupa and its display of ancient Isan artifacts
The meditating Buddha under a naga hood, said to be brought from Ayutthaya
blocks.bestFor: Merit-makers and temple-goers who enjoy a beautiful, quiet temple
blocks.hours: Open daily during the day (approx. 6:00 am-6:00 pm)

blocks.name: Yasothon Red Lotus Field
blocks.area: Ban Samrong, Khu Mueang Subdistrict, Maha Chana Chai District, Yasothon
blocks.signature: Over 100 rai of blooming red lotus, the province's signature flower, best seen in the morning 5:00-11:00 am from December to February
blocks.descHtml:
If you love the quiet atmosphere of rural Isan paired with natural scenery beautiful enough to stop you in your tracks, the red lotus field at Ban Samrong deserves a spot on your list. It's a natural wetland originally called "Nong Loeng," in Ban Samrong, Khu Mueang Subdistrict, Maha Chana Chai District, Yasothon, where red lotuses grow wild across more than 90 rai of water. Local villagers and the community have worked together to develop it into a conservation-based tourist spot — a great fit for photographers, nature lovers, and families wanting to bring older relatives for a relaxed stroll in the cool morning air.

The must-see highlight is taking a boat out into the middle of the wetland, surrounded by pink-red lotus blooms as far as the eye can see — this red lotus happens to be Yasothon's provincial flower. Along the way you'll often spot flocks of waterbirds flying close by. Some visitors choose to cycle or ride a saleng (motorised trike) around the wetland instead. Real visitor reviews consistently say an early-morning visit is well worth it — beautiful light, lotuses in full bloom, and pleasant weather. If you're hungry, there's hot khao chi (grilled sticky rice), coffee, and local handwoven silk to pick up on your way out.

Budget-wise, it's very easy on the wallet — free parking, with the boat/entry fee running only about 10-20 baht. It's located in Maha Chana Chai District, a fair distance from Yasothon city, so driving yourself is recommended. The lotuses bloom most beautifully in the cool season, roughly December to February, and you'll need to visit in the morning, from about 5:00-11:00 am, since the blooms start closing after midday. The field's popularity comes from the sheer scale of a wetland covered in pink lotus, easy to reach and stunning to see — it's Yasothon's signature cool-season check-in spot.

One thing to know: the red lotus bloom is a seasonal phenomenon. Outside the cool season, the flowers may not bloom, and in some years the water level drops because it's pumped out for rice farming, so it's worth checking a local page for the current bloom status before heading out — and go early to beat the heat and catch the flowers at their fullest.
mustOrder: Boat ride through the red lotus field
Spot flocks of waterbirds
Ride a saleng trike or cycle around the wetland
Hot khao chi with coffee
blocks.bestFor: An early-morning outing in the cool breeze, watching the lotus in full bloom at year's end

blocks.name: Phu Phra Cave
blocks.area: Kut Hae Subdistrict, Loeng Nok Tha District
blocks.signature: A limestone cave enshrining Buddha images and a Buddha footprint, in a shaded, peaceful setting
blocks.descHtml:
If you enjoy a mix of dharma and light adventure, Phu Phra Cave is a spot Yasothon locals take real pride in. It's a rock cave on the Phu Phra mountain range enshrining rows of ancient Buddha images, including a reclining Buddha and two Phra Sangkajai images, said to have been created around 1957 during the era of Phra Achan Dee Chanoto. The surrounding forest spans roughly 200 rai of mixed deciduous woodland, shaded and cool — a good fit for anyone seeking a quiet spot to pay respects, meditate, or bring the family for a light, easy forest walk near the city.

The must-see highlight is the inner Phu Phra cave itself, a natural two-level cave set into a rock outcrop on the southern side of the mountain. Deeper inside are rows of ancient Buddha images that many reviewers describe as genuinely striking and sacred. A short climb further up leads to a viewpoint overlooking the forest and mountain range stretching into the distance. Nearby are several other caves worth following up on, including Tham Kliang, Tham Keng, and Tham Phrommabut — a great itinerary for anyone wanting to see it all in one trip.

Budget-wise, there's nothing to worry about, since entry is completely free. It's open roughly 6:00 am-5:00 pm daily, located in Kut Hae Subdistrict, Loeng Nok Tha District, about 12 km from Loeng Nok Tha town and about 85 km from Yasothon city. The road in is easy to drive, though once you park, there's a fair amount of walking up and down.

A few things past visitors mention: the path into the cave is fairly steep and rocky, so wear sneakers or shoes with good grip, bring water, and be extra careful in the rainy season when the path gets slippery. Morning or late afternoon makes for the most comfortable walk, since the forest air is still cool and the sun isn't too strong.
mustOrder: The inner cave enshrining rows of ancient Buddha images
The reclining Buddha and two Phra Sangkajai images
The mountain viewpoint over the forest and ranges
Nearby Tham Kliang, Tham Keng, and Tham Phrommabut caves
blocks.bestFor: Spiritually-minded nature lovers wanting to pay respects in a cave and hike near the city

blocks.name: Ban Song Peuay Ancient Site (Dong Mueang Toei)
blocks.area: Ban Song Peuay, Kham Khuean Kaeo District, Yasothon
blocks.signature: The ancient community of Dong Mueang Toei, with old Buddha images and traces of the Khmer-Dvaravati era, tied to the Kong Khao Noi legend
blocks.descHtml:
If you're into quiet history without having to fight anyone for a photo spot, "Dong Mueang Toei" in Ban Song Peuay, Kham Khuean Kaeo District, deserves a spot on the Yasothon list. This isn't a beautiful temple or a picture-perfect landmark, but the remains of a genuinely ancient city. An oval-shaped earthen mound is ringed by a moat and earthen rampart, and at its centre stand the remains of a brick tower — built without mortar — standing about 1.7 metres tall, a genuine relic from the pre-Angkorian (Chenla) era, roughly the 7th-8th century Buddhist Era, showing early Khmer artistic influence. It's a great fit for anyone wanting to experience a deeper side of Isan than usual.

The must-see highlight is the brick tower remains at the centre of the mound, along with the story of the Dong Mueang Toei inscription, written in Pallava script in Sanskrit, which states that the site was originally a Brahmanical religious site before later converting to Buddhism. Around the area, fragments of Dvaravati-era earthenware, pieces of a face-shaped window ornament (kudu), and stone lions have also been found. Interestingly, locals link this site to the "Kong Khao Noi Kha Mae" legend, since Phra That Kong Khao Noi is in the same province. Reading the Fine Arts Department's information panels as you walk feels like flipping through a history textbook in the middle of an open field.

Cost-wise, there's nothing to worry about — entry is free, since the site sits within the Dong Mueang Toei monastic forest grounds, open daily during the daytime with no ticket booth. To get there from Yasothon city, take Highway 23 (Chaeng Sanit) south for about 20 km, then turn into Ban Song Peuay for another 5 km. A sedan can make it in, though a private vehicle is recommended since public transport isn't convenient.

One thing to know before you go: this is a raw, unpolished ancient site, not an air-conditioned museum. The grass may be overgrown in places and the information panels are modest rather than flashy. If you're expecting a grand check-in spot, you may find it underwhelming, but if you come with genuine curiosity about history, it's well worth the visit. The province is currently working to develop it as a historical tourism site, and the village also has an agro-tourism project with fruit orchards you can visit afterwards. We'd recommend going in the morning or evening when the sun is gentler, wearing comfortable walking shoes, and bringing water.

blocks.text: Many of Yasothon's attractions sit in different districts — the Song Yae wooden church in Thai Charoen, the red lotus field in Maha Chana Chai, and Phu Phra Cave in Loeng Nok Tha. If you'd rather not drive yourself, or just want a guide to handle the logistics, check out province-wide tour packages and Isan tours on Klook or GetYourGuide — book tickets and activities in advance so you don't have to queue on the day. Time your trip to the red lotus season so you catch the blooms at their best.

blocks.title: Know Before You Go to Yasothon

items.title: Driving yourself or renting a car is easiest
items.text: Attractions in central Yasothon are within walking distance of each other, but the Song Yae wooden church, the red lotus field, and Phu Phra Cave are all outside town in different directions, and public transport is limited. The most convenient option is to rent a car or motorbike — Grab is barely available in Yasothon, so arrange transport before heading out of town.

items.title: Carry cash
items.text: Temples, the donation box at Song Yae church, entry to the Phaya Khankhak Museum, and boat/transport fares at the red lotus field are mostly cash-only. Keep small bills handy for entry fees, parking, and roadside food. ATMs are easy to find in the city centre but scarce at outlying attractions.

items.title: See the red lotus field in the morning, and in season
items.text: The red lotus field blooms beautifully in the morning, roughly 5:00-11:00 am, and only during the cool season from December to February. Visit outside that window and you won't see any flowers. Phaya Thaen Park, on the other hand, is enjoyable year-round and most comfortable in the cool evening breeze. Time your trip to the season for the best experience.

items.title: Dress modestly at temples and churches
items.text: Wat Mahathat, Wat Phra Phutthabat Yasothon, Phu Phra Cave, and Ban Song Yae Christian Church are sacred sites where people genuinely come to make merit and pray. Cover shoulders and knees, remove shoes where signs indicate, and keep your voice down inside the halls and the church.

items.title: English is limited
items.text: Outside the major tourist spots, English signage and menus are scarce. Bring a translation app, or point at pictures at markets and restaurants to communicate — most Yasothon locals are kind and patient with visitors.

items.title: Phaya Khankhak and the Bun Bang Fai festival are the local claim to fame
items.text: Yasothon is famous for the Bun Bang Fai rocket festival, held every year around May. The Phaya Khankhak (toad) legend told at the museum comes from this very tradition. If you visit during the festival, expect a lively procession and rocket-launching that's especially spirited.

blocks.title: Planning the Most of Your Yasothon Trip
blocks.html:
Yasothon is easy to explore because the city's highlights cluster around Phaya Thaen Park — take a walk by the water in the cool breeze, then visit the giant-toad Phaya Khankhak Museum right next door in the same area. From there, head into the municipal area to photograph the colourful Sino-European buildings of the Ban Sing Tha old town, and stop to pay respects to Phra That Anon and the Dewdrop Buddha at Wat Mahathat, the city's guardian temple. A half day is enough to cover the city centre. Phra That Kong Khao Noi is just outside town in Tat Thong Subdistrict, an easy detour along the way.

If you have more than a day, drive out of town. For the faithful and architecture lovers, head to Ban Song Yae Christian Church in Thai Charoen District, Thailand's largest wooden church, then continue toward Maha Chana Chai to pay respects to the white jade Buddha at Wat Phra Phutthabat Yasothon, followed by the red lotus field at Ban Samrong, which blooms beautifully from early morning through the cool season into early the following year. For quiet nature, head to Phu Phra Cave in Loeng Nok Tha; for history, stop at Dong Mueang Toei, the ancient community in Kham Khuean Kaeo, and the Ho Trai scripture library on the water at Wat Sa Trai Nurak in Sai Mun. Plan your out-of-town route in one direction to save the most time.

blocks.text: A day trip to Yasothon is plenty of fun, but staying a night in the city means you can stroll by Phaya Thaen Park in the evening, visit the giant-toad museum while it's quiet, then head out the next morning to catch the red lotus field or the Song Yae wooden church. Compare Yasothon hotel prices and reviews before you book.

faq.q: What are the must-see attractions in Yasothon?
faq.a: The spots people never skip in Yasothon are the Phaya Khankhak Museum (Vimarn Phaya Thaen), a 19-metre giant-toad building that tells the Bun Bang Fai legend; Phra That Kong Khao Noi, an old stupa standing amid rice fields tied to the 'child who killed his mother' legend; the Ban Sing Tha old town with its brightly coloured Sino-European buildings; Wat Mahathat, home to Phra That Anon and the Dewdrop Buddha; and Ban Song Yae Christian Church, Thailand's largest wooden church, in Thai Charoen District.

faq.q: What is Yasothon best known for?
faq.a: Yasothon's highlights are the stories and legends woven into its attractions — from the giant-toad Phaya Khankhak Museum, as tall as a five-storey building and tied to the province's famous Bun Bang Fai rocket festival, standing beside the golden Vimarn Phaya Thaen, to Phra That Kong Khao Noi, shaped like a rice basket amid the fields per local folklore, and the Ban Sing Tha old town, where pastel Sino-European shophouses have become a popular retro photo spot. For the faithful, there's also the Song Yae wooden church, Thailand's largest, built entirely of hardwood.

faq.q: Are Yasothon's attractions expensive to visit?
faq.a: Most are free or very cheap. Phra That Kong Khao Noi, the Ban Sing Tha old town, the Ho Trai scripture library at Wat Sa Trai Nurak, Wat Mahathat, Wat Phra Phutthabat Yasothon, Phu Phra Cave, and Dong Mueang Toei are all free to enter. Ban Song Yae Christian Church is free with a donation box, while the Phaya Khankhak Museum charges around 40 baht for adults and 20 baht for children, and the red lotus field has free parking with only a small boat or transport fee of about 20 baht.

faq.q: How do I get around Yasothon, and is parking easy?
faq.a: Yasothon is reachable by bus from Bangkok, or onward from Ubon Ratchathani or Roi Et airport, but once you're there, driving yourself or renting a car is by far the most convenient option since public transport within the province is limited. City-centre attractions like the Phaya Khankhak Museum, Ban Sing Tha, and Wat Mahathat are close together with parking available. The Song Yae wooden church in Thai Charoen, the red lotus field and Wat Phra Phutthabat in Maha Chana Chai, Phu Phra Cave in Loeng Nok Tha, and the Ho Trai scripture library in Sai Mun are all outside town in different directions, so arrange transport before heading out.

faq.q: What are the opening hours for Yasothon's attractions?
faq.a: The Phaya Khankhak Museum keeps set daytime hours, and the Ho Trai scripture library at Sai Mun is open for viewing during the day. Temples like Wat Mahathat, Wat Phra Phutthabat Yasothon, and Phu Phra Cave are open from morning to evening — visiting early means fewer crowds and softer sun. The red lotus field blooms best in the morning, roughly 5:00-11:00 am, and only flowers during the cool season from December to February. It's best to check the hours and season for each spot before you set out, since they may shift around public holidays.
